items.title: Tailwind CSS: utility-first styling and how it is wired in our apps
items.body:
Tailwind CSS is a utility-first styling tool. Instead of writing a class like .nav-link in a stylesheet, you compose small single-purpose classes directly in the markup: flex, items-center, gap-5, px-4, text-sm. The build scans your source files, finds the class names you used, and generates only that CSS, so the shipped stylesheet stays small. States and breakpoints are prefixes: hover:text-white, md:grid-cols-2.

Both gglearn and ggsocial list tailwindcss and @tailwindcss/postcss in package.json with a caret range of 4 (the major version is 4; we do not pin the minor here). Each has a postcss.config.mjs that registers the @tailwindcss/postcss plugin, and neither has a tailwind.config file. Configuration is CSS-first: app/globals.css starts with @import "tailwindcss" and customises the theme inside the CSS itself. For example gglearn's layout writes the header as one string of utilities such as sticky top-0 z-40 border-b border-white/10 backdrop-blur, and links as text-slate-300 transition hover:text-white. The trade-off is long class strings in components, which is why repeated patterns get extracted into components or a few named classes.

items.title: Theme tokens: CSS variables mapped into Tailwind with @theme
items.body:
Hard-coding colours in every component makes restyling painful. Our apps instead define design tokens as CSS variables and expose them to Tailwind with an @theme block. In ggsocial's globals.css, :root defines --bg, --surface, --border, --text, --muted, --accent, --ok, --warn, --danger and three chart colours. A later @theme inline block maps them: --color-surface: var(--surface), and so on. Because of that mapping, utilities such as bg-surface-2, text-muted, border-border and text-accent-fg exist, and components in the layout use them.

The inline keyword tells Tailwind to reference the variable itself rather than copy its value, so changing the variable at runtime changes every utility that uses it. That is what makes theming cheap.

gglearn does the same on a smaller scale: :root sets --background and --foreground, and @theme inline maps them to color-background and color-foreground. It also uses some one-off values in classes, such as bg-[#070b1a]/80 and text-[11px]. Arbitrary values in square brackets are fine occasionally, but if a value repeats, promote it to a token so it has one place to change.

questions.prompt: In ggsocial, how does a token like --surface-2 become a usable class such as bg-surface-2?

options.text: It is copied into package.json
A PM2 setting generates it
Tailwind guesses it from the variable name
An @theme inline block maps --color-surface-2 to var(--surface-2)

questions.prompt: What is the benefit of defining colours as CSS variables behind the utilities?

options.text: Changing the variable at runtime restyles every utility that uses it
Browsers refuse to cache the stylesheet
It removes the need for PostCSS
The HTML becomes smaller than any other option

questions.prompt: A gglearn class uses bg-[#070b1a]/80. What is this called, and when is it a smell?

options.text: A breakpoint; when it is used on mobile
An arbitrary value; when the same value repeats and should be a token
A plugin; when it is not installed
A layer; when it is unlayered

questions.prompt: Your team wants a new 'info' colour used in 30 places in ggsocial. Describe step by step how to add it so that dark mode keeps working.
questions.answer: Define --info in :root, give a dark-adjusted value in the prefers-color-scheme dark block (the :root:not([data-theme="light"]) rule), then add --color-info: var(--info) in the @theme inline block. Use text-info or bg-info in components. Check contrast against --surface in both themes. Do not hard-code a hex in the 30 places.
questions.rubric: Must cover :root var, dark override, @theme inline mapping, using utility, contrast check.

items.title: Dark mode and component patterns: two different approaches
items.body:
The two apps handle dark mode differently, which is a useful comparison. gglearn is dark-only: its :root background is a deep navy, the body uses layered gradients, and we found no dark: variant classes in its components. There is no light theme to switch to, so no toggle is needed.

ggsocial follows the user's system. Its light token values sit in :root, and a media query for prefers-color-scheme: dark overrides them inside :root:not([data-theme="light"]). The data-theme attribute lets a user force light even when the OS is dark. Dark values are stepped on purpose, not just inverted: a comment explains the dark accent is a light violet, so text on it switches to a dark colour for contrast. Components never mention dark: because they use token utilities that change with the variables.

For component patterns, gglearn keeps repeated looks as named classes in globals.css (.card, .btn, .gradient-text) and keeps layout as utilities. ggsocial keeps its own Card, Button and Field in components/ui.tsx, built from utilities, and uses a shared gg-ui kit copied from another repo. Prefer React components over copying long class strings.
items.source: gglearn/app/globals.css; ggsocial/src/app/globals.css; ggsocial/README.md; ggsocial/src/components (ui.tsx referenced in README)

questions.prompt: Compare how gglearn and ggsocial approach dark mode, and say why dark values should be stepped rather than just inverted.
questions.answer: gglearn is dark-only: dark navy background and gradients set in globals.css, with no dark: variants and no toggle. ggsocial defines light tokens in :root and overrides them in a prefers-color-scheme dark block guarded by :root:not([data-theme="light"]), so the OS preference applies unless the user forces light. Dark values must be chosen for contrast on dark surfaces; for example the dark accent is a light violet, so text on it is made dark, because simply inverting would give poor contrast (white on it was only about 3:1 per the comment).

questions.prompt: You are adding a settings page to gglearn that needs a repeated card-with-button look. Where would you put the styling and why?
questions.answer: Reuse the existing .card and .btn classes from globals.css where they fit, and use utilities only for layout (flex, gap, padding). If the page needs a new repeated look, create a small React component or a named class rather than pasting long utility strings into many files. Keep colours on tokens or existing classes so a later restyle touches one place.
questions.rubric: Must favour reuse of existing classes/components, utilities for layout, avoid duplicated strings, tokens.

items.title: Tailwind pitfalls we have actually hit
items.body:
Our repos record concrete Tailwind traps. First, CSS layering. ggsocial's globals.css warns that everything below a point must stay inside @layer base. Unlayered rules beat every Tailwind utility regardless of specificity, so an unlayered rule like button { color: inherit } silently overrides text-accent-fg and leaves dark text on an accent fill. Note gglearn's named classes (.card, .btn) are written outside any layer in its globals.css as we saw it, so they would override a utility on the same property; keep that in mind when mixing them.

Second, preflight, Tailwind's reset of browser defaults. ggsocial's README says to import the shared kit's styles.css only and never base.css, which would fight preflight.

Third, deployment. ggsocial's DEPLOY.md says npm ci silently skips the Linux native Tailwind binary (@tailwindcss/oxide-linux-x64-gnu) because the lockfile was generated on macOS, so the server build fails with a cannot-find-module error. The fix is an explicit npm install with --no-save pinned to the installed oxide version, keeping the platform artefact out of the lockfile. It also notes that Turbopack can cache a failed build.

Finally, dynamically built class names like text-${color}-500 are not found by the scanner; use full class names.
items.source: ggsocial/src/app/globals.css (layer comment); ggsocial/README.md; ggsocial/DEPLOY.md; gglearn/app/globals.css; general practice
